channel.title: Abracadabra AI blog
channel.description: Notes on AI readiness and small-business adoption. A post appears here on its publish date.

item.title: AI Agents for Business: When to Use One
item.description: Eight jobs can sit with an agent only when a person still checks the output. Anthropic says to start simpler. Gartner expects many agent projects to be canceled.

item.title: AI Agents vs Agentic AI: A Plain Split
item.description: An agent takes a goal and chooses tools. Agentic AI is the wider bet, and many of those projects are forecast to be canceled. Start with a workflow.

item.title: AI Automation Agency vs Consultant: Who to Hire
item.description: Hire a consultant to name the job. Hire an agency to build after the job is named. Training plans and scaling rates are both thinner than use.

item.title: AI Automation for Small Business: Which Job First
item.description: Pick the first job by volume, how stable the rules are, whether the data can be read, and what a wrong answer costs. Surveys show which jobs already appear.

item.title: AI Consultant for Small Business: What to Ask
item.description: A useful consultant names the job, the data, and the stop. Most firms use AI somewhere. Far fewer are scaling agents. Guaranteed rankings are a red flag.

item.title: AI for Small Business: What the Surveys Still Say
item.description: Two surveys still disagree because they ask different questions. One counts generative AI use. The other counts AI used to produce the goods or the service.

item.title: An AI Implementation Framework in Five Stages
item.description: Name the job, score the data, write the process, assign a checker, then keep or stop. Surveys show use is common and scaling is not.

item.title: AI Readiness Assessment Questionnaire: The Themes
item.description: Ask about data, process, people, and the decision before you ask about a tool. A public checklist does not publish a readiness rate for small firms.

item.title: AI Readiness Assessment: What It Measures and How to Score
item.description: An AI readiness assessment scores data, process, people, and decisions. Compare public tools, then read what each Readiness Check band means.

item.title: AI Readiness Checklist Before You Buy a Tool
item.description: Questions to answer before you buy an AI tool, grouped by data, process, people, and the decision. Public surveys name the gaps those questions catch.

item.title: An AI Readiness Framework an Owner Can Score
item.description: Score data, process, people, and the decision in words, then read the band. Public research names the gaps. The check names the one that is yours.

item.title: AI-Ready Data: What a Small Business Needs First
item.description: AI-ready data means one current source for the job, readable by a system. Gartner's figures describe the firms that do not have that yet.

item.title: AI Strategy for Small Business: Start With the Job
item.description: Name the job, the data, and who checks the output before you buy a tool. Use is already common. A written plan and staff training are not.

item.title: Answer Engine Optimization: What Google Still Requires
item.description: Google still treats answer-engine work as ordinary SEO. A research paper reports visibility gains. Pew found fewer clicks when a summary appears.

item.title: Business Process Automation With AI: Write the Job
item.description: Write the steps before you add a model. Most knowledge workers already use AI. Few companies were planning training. Many proofs of concept still stop.

item.title: Generative Engine Optimization vs SEO
item.description: Google says the new names are still SEO. A research paper measures visibility. Pew measured the click. Write the page so both can use it.

item.title: How Can AI Help a Small Business? What Surveys Count
item.description: Two 2025 surveys count different work. This note separates generative-AI use from AI in production, then names the jobs owners hand over.

item.title: How to Show Up in ChatGPT and AI Overviews
item.description: Showing up in ChatGPT search is a crawler and indexing problem. Google still treats answer-engine advice as ordinary SEO. Clicks fall when a summary appears.

item.title: How to Use AI in Your Business: Twelve Jobs
item.description: Pick a job you already do, write the steps, and keep a person on the output. A Canadian survey shows which uses, and which follow-on work, are common.

item.title: Is My Business Ready for AI? Signs to Read First
item.description: Ready means the data, the process, the people, and the decision can carry a tool. This note reads the Check bands against a large-firm index.

item.title: Off-the-Shelf AI or Custom Software
item.description: Buy the product when it already does the job. Build only when the job is yours alone. Surveys show generative AI use is already common among small firms.

item.title: What Is an AI Agent? A Plain Answer for Owners
item.description: An agent picks its own next step. A workflow follows a path you wrote. This note uses Anthropic's distinction and McKinsey's survey of who is scaling.

item.title: What Is llms.txt, and Who Actually Reads It
item.description: A proposed file that points models at your best pages. Google says it does not use the file. A large study found most copies are never requested.

item.title: Why AI Pilots Stall After the Demo
item.description: Pilots stall when the data, the risk controls, or the value was never named. Surveys show use is common and scaling is rare. The demo is not the process.
